software-engineer.title: Software Engineer
software-engineer.description: Designs, builds, tests and maintains software applications and systems.

data-analyst.title: Data Analyst
data-analyst.description: Turns raw data into reports, dashboards and insights that guide business decisions.

product-manager.title: Product Manager
product-manager.description: Decides what a product should do and aligns engineering, design and business teams to deliver it.

ux-designer.title: UX Designer
ux-designer.description: Researches user needs and designs intuitive flows, wireframes and interfaces for digital products.

devops-engineer.title: DevOps Engineer
devops-engineer.description: Automates infrastructure, deployments and monitoring so software ships reliably and quickly.

nurse.title: Nurse
nurse.description: Provides direct patient care, administers treatments and coordinates with doctors and families.

pharmacist.title: Pharmacist
pharmacist.description: Dispenses medicines safely and advises patients and clinicians on dosage, interactions and side effects.

physiotherapist.title: Physiotherapist
physiotherapist.description: Helps patients recover movement and manage pain through exercise, manual therapy and education.

accountant.title: Accountant
accountant.description: Prepares financial statements, manages ledgers and ensures tax and reporting compliance.

financial-analyst.title: Financial Analyst
financial-analyst.description: Builds forecasts and financial models to evaluate performance, budgets and investment decisions.

hr-specialist.title: HR Specialist
hr-specialist.description: Handles recruitment, onboarding, employee relations and HR policies within an organization.

project-manager.title: Project Manager
project-manager.description: Plans projects, manages scope, budget and timelines, and keeps stakeholders aligned until delivery.

lawyer.title: Lawyer
lawyer.description: Advises clients on legal matters, drafts contracts and represents them in negotiations or court.

sales-representative.title: Sales Representative
sales-representative.description: Finds and qualifies prospects, presents products and closes deals to meet revenue targets.

digital-marketing-specialist.title: Digital Marketing Specialist
digital-marketing-specialist.description: Plans and optimizes online campaigns across search, social, email and paid channels.

teacher.title: Teacher
teacher.description: Plans lessons, teaches students and assesses their progress in a school setting.

civil-engineer.title: Civil Engineer
civil-engineer.description: Designs and supervises infrastructure such as roads, bridges, buildings and water systems.

mechanical-engineer.title: Mechanical Engineer
mechanical-engineer.description: Designs, analyzes and improves machines, products and manufacturing processes.

electrical-engineer.title: Electrical Engineer
electrical-engineer.description: Designs and tests electrical systems, from power distribution to electronics and controls.

graphic-designer.title: Graphic Designer
graphic-designer.description: Creates visual concepts for brands, marketing materials, websites and publications.

architect.title: Architect
architect.description: Designs buildings and spaces, balancing aesthetics, function, regulations and budget.

customer-support-specialist.title: Customer Support Specialist
customer-support-specialist.description: Resolves customer questions and problems by phone, chat or email and keeps customers satisfied.

hotel-manager.title: Hotel Manager
hotel-manager.description: Oversees hotel operations, staff, guest experience and financial performance.

chef.title: Chef
chef.description: Plans menus, prepares dishes and runs the kitchen team to consistent quality standards.

united-states.name: United States
united-states.summary: The United States is the world's largest economy, with a dynamic and highly competitive job market. Pay is often high, but benefits such as health insurance and paid leave vary a lot by employer.
united-states.jobMarket: Technology, healthcare, finance and professional services consistently hire at scale. Engineering, data, cybersecurity and nursing roles remain in strong demand across many states.
united-states.visa: Common routes include the H-1B specialty occupation visa, L-1 intra-company transfers, O-1 for exceptional ability, and employment-based green cards. Most routes require employer sponsorship and some use lotteries, so always check the official USCIS and State Department websites, as rules change often.
united-states.salaryNote: Salaries vary widely by city and state, with coastal tech hubs paying the most. Always factor in healthcare costs, taxes and bonuses or equity when comparing offers.
tips: Keep your résumé to one or two pages and leave out photos, age and marital status.
Quantify achievements with numbers, percentages and results.
Expect behavioral questions and answer them with clear STAR-style stories.
Confidently talking about your own contributions is expected, not seen as boasting.

canada.name: Canada
canada.summary: Canada has a stable, diverse economy and actively welcomes skilled immigrants. Major hubs include Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal and Calgary.
canada.jobMarket: Healthcare, technology, skilled trades, engineering and finance are key hiring sectors. Many provinces report shortages in nursing, construction and IT roles.
canada.visa: Skilled workers often apply for permanent residence through Express Entry or Provincial Nominee Programs, while employer-specific work permits may require a labour market assessment. Programs and selection criteria change frequently, so check the official Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) website.
canada.salaryNote: Salaries are generally lower than in the US but come with public healthcare. Pay and cost of living differ significantly between provinces and cities.
canada.languages: English and French (French is essential in much of Quebec)
tips: Use a one- or two-page résumé without a photo, date of birth or marital status.
Canadian employers value relevant local or transferable experience, so highlight it clearly.
Politeness and a collaborative tone matter; avoid overly aggressive self-promotion.
Prepare references in advance, as they are commonly checked.

united-kingdom.name: United Kingdom
united-kingdom.summary: The United Kingdom has a large services-driven economy with London as a global centre for finance and technology. Cities like Manchester, Edinburgh and Bristol also have growing job markets.
united-kingdom.jobMarket: Finance, technology, healthcare (especially the NHS), engineering and creative industries are major employers. Health and social care, software and data roles appear frequently on shortage lists.
united-kingdom.visa: The main route is the Skilled Worker visa, which requires a job offer from a licensed sponsor that meets salary and skill thresholds. There are also Health and Care Worker, Global Talent and Graduate routes; check GOV.UK for current requirements, as thresholds are updated regularly.
united-kingdom.salaryNote: London salaries are notably higher but so is the cost of living. Salaries are usually quoted as annual gross before income tax and National Insurance.
tips: Keep your CV to about two pages and don't include a photo.
Use competency-based examples, since many interviews follow that format.
A modest, understated tone works better than hard selling.
Add a short, tailored cover letter when the application allows it.

ireland.name: Ireland
ireland.summary: Ireland is an English-speaking EU country that hosts the European headquarters of many global tech and pharma companies. Most opportunities are concentrated in Dublin, Cork and Galway.
ireland.jobMarket: Technology, pharmaceuticals, medical devices, finance and aircraft leasing are major sectors. Software engineering, data, healthcare and construction roles are in steady demand.
ireland.visa: Non-EU professionals commonly use the Critical Skills Employment Permit for in-demand occupations or the General Employment Permit for other roles. Eligibility lists and salary thresholds are reviewed regularly, so check the official Department of Enterprise and Irish Immigration Service websites.
ireland.salaryNote: Salaries in tech and pharma are competitive by European standards. Housing costs in Dublin are high, so weigh rent carefully when comparing offers.
ireland.languages: English (Irish is an official language but rarely required at work)
tips: Use a concise two-page CV without a photo.
Friendly small talk at the start of an interview is common; relax and engage.
Show genuine interest in the company's work in Ireland, not only the global brand.
Competency-based questions are common, so prepare structured examples.

germany.name: Germany
germany.summary: Germany is Europe's largest economy, known for engineering, manufacturing and a strong Mittelstand of mid-sized firms. Berlin, Munich, Hamburg and Frankfurt are major job hubs.
germany.jobMarket: Automotive, mechanical and electrical engineering, IT, healthcare and skilled trades all face talent shortages. Nursing, software development and engineering roles are especially sought after.
germany.visa: Key routes are the EU Blue Card for qualified professionals meeting a salary threshold, the skilled worker visa, and the Opportunity Card for job seekers. Requirements such as recognised qualifications and salary levels change, so check the official Make it in Germany portal and German missions abroad.
germany.salaryNote: Salaries are usually quoted as annual gross, and taxes plus social contributions are significant. Pay tends to be higher in the south and in large cities.
germany.languages: German (English is common in tech and startups, but German greatly widens your options)
tips: A tabular CV (Lebenslauf) is standard; a professional photo is optional but still common.
Include certificates and references (Arbeitszeugnisse) in your application if you have them.
Be punctual and precise; interviews tend to be structured and fact-focused.
Expect detailed questions about your qualifications and exactly what you did in each role.

netherlands.name: Netherlands
netherlands.summary: The Netherlands has an open, international economy with a high share of English speakers. Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague and Eindhoven host many multinational employers.
netherlands.jobMarket: Technology, logistics, agri-food, life sciences, high-tech manufacturing and finance are strong sectors. Software, data, engineering and healthcare roles are in demand.
netherlands.visa: Many professionals come through the Highly Skilled Migrant scheme, which requires an employer recognised by the immigration service and a minimum salary, or through the EU Blue Card. Rules and thresholds are updated regularly, so check the official IND website.
netherlands.salaryNote: Salaries are usually quoted as annual gross and often include a holiday allowance. Housing costs in the Randstad area can be high.
netherlands.languages: Dutch and English (English is widely used in international companies)
tips: Keep your CV short and factual; a photo is optional.
Dutch communication is direct, so give clear and honest answers.
Show you can work independently and contribute to consensus-based decisions.
Don't overstate achievements; modest but concrete examples land well.

switzerland.name: Switzerland
switzerland.summary: Switzerland offers some of the highest salaries in the world, a stable economy and a very high quality of life. Zurich, Geneva, Basel and Lausanne are the main job centres.
switzerland.jobMarket: Banking, insurance, pharmaceuticals, precision engineering, IT and international organisations are major employers. Specialists in tech, life sciences and finance are especially sought after.
switzerland.visa: EU/EFTA citizens benefit from free movement, while non-EU nationals face annual quotas and must usually be highly qualified, with the employer showing no suitable local candidate was found. Check the official State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) and cantonal authority websites for current rules.
switzerland.salaryNote: Salaries are very high, but so are rents, health insurance and daily costs. Pay levels also differ between cantons and language regions.
switzerland.languages: German, French and Italian depending on region; English is common in multinationals
tips: A complete application often includes a CV with photo, certificates and reference letters.
Precision and reliability are valued; double-check every detail in your documents.
Punctuality is essential; arrive a few minutes early.
Learning the local language of the region is a strong advantage.

luxembourg.name: Luxembourg
luxembourg.summary: Luxembourg is a small but wealthy EU country with one of the highest average incomes in Europe. A large share of its workforce commutes daily from neighbouring France, Belgium and Germany.
luxembourg.jobMarket: Financial services, fund administration, banking, EU institutions, IT and logistics dominate. Compliance, accounting, IT and multilingual professionals are in high demand.
luxembourg.visa: EU citizens can work freely, while non-EU professionals typically use the EU Blue Card or a salaried worker residence permit tied to a job offer. Requirements change, so check the official Guichet.lu portal and the immigration directorate.
luxembourg.salaryNote: Salaries are among the highest in the EU, supported by a high statutory minimum wage. Housing is expensive, which is why many people live across the border.
luxembourg.languages: Luxembourgish, French and German; English is widely used in finance
tips: Highlight all the languages you speak, as multilingualism is a major asset.
Tailor your CV to the finance or EU context if relevant, with precise dates and responsibilities.
Interviews can switch languages, so be ready to answer in more than one.
A formal, polished presentation is expected in finance and institutional roles.

sweden.name: Sweden
sweden.summary: Sweden has an innovative economy known for global brands, startups and a strong focus on work-life balance. Stockholm, Gothenburg and Malmö are the main job hubs.
sweden.jobMarket: Technology, gaming, clean energy, life sciences, engineering and healthcare are key sectors. Software developers, engineers and healthcare staff are in demand.
sweden.visa: Non-EU professionals usually need a work permit based on a job offer that meets salary and employment-condition requirements, and some may qualify for the EU Blue Card. Rules have been tightened in recent years, so check the official Swedish Migration Agency (Migrationsverket) website.
sweden.salaryNote: Salaries are moderate by Western European standards, but benefits, parental leave and holidays are generous. Taxes are relatively high.
sweden.languages: Swedish (English is widely spoken, especially in tech)
tips: Keep your CV concise; a photo is optional.
Swedish workplaces are flat, so show teamwork and humility rather than hierarchy.
Avoid exaggeration; balanced, honest answers build trust.
Expect questions about how you collaborate and make decisions together.

denmark.name: Denmark
denmark.summary: Denmark combines a strong economy with high trust, flexible labour rules and excellent work-life balance. Copenhagen and Aarhus are the main employment centres.
denmark.jobMarket: Life sciences, green energy, shipping, IT and engineering are key sectors. Healthcare professionals, engineers and IT specialists are frequently in demand.
denmark.visa: Common routes include the Pay Limit Scheme for well-paid job offers, the Positive List for shortage occupations, and fast-track schemes for certified employers. Check the official New to Denmark (SIRI) website, as schemes and thresholds change.
denmark.salaryNote: Salaries are high but so are income taxes, which fund extensive public services. Most employees have generous paid holidays.
denmark.languages: Danish (English is widely used in international companies)
tips: Write a short, personal CV and a tailored motivation letter.
Danish culture is informal and egalitarian, so be relaxed but professional.
Show that you work independently and take responsibility.
Be honest about what you don't know; overselling can backfire.

australia.name: Australia
australia.summary: Australia has a strong economy, a high standard of living and a long history of skilled migration. Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth are major job markets.
australia.jobMarket: Healthcare, construction, mining and resources, education and technology are major employers. Nurses, engineers, tradespeople and IT professionals often appear on skills shortage lists.
australia.visa: Options include employer-sponsored temporary and permanent visas, and points-based skilled independent or state-nominated visas. Occupation lists and requirements change regularly, so check the official Department of Home Affairs website.
australia.salaryNote: Salaries are generally high and employers pay mandatory superannuation (retirement contributions) on top. Costs in Sydney and Melbourne are high, especially housing.
tips: A résumé of two to three pages is common; no photo is needed.
Use a friendly, down-to-earth tone; arrogance is quickly noticed.
Prepare behavioral examples using the STAR method.
Show that you understand local standards or licensing if your field requires them.

united-arab-emirates.name: United Arab Emirates
united-arab-emirates.summary: The United Arab Emirates is a regional business hub with a large international workforce. Dubai and Abu Dhabi attract professionals from all over the world.
united-arab-emirates.jobMarket: Finance, real estate, construction, tourism and hospitality, aviation, logistics and technology are major sectors. Demand is growing in AI, fintech and renewable energy.
united-arab-emirates.visa: Most professionals work under an employer-sponsored work permit and residence visa, and there are also Golden Visa and Green Visa options for certain skilled or high-earning people. Check official government portals such as u.ae and the relevant emirate authorities, as rules change.
united-arab-emirates.salaryNote: Many jobs pay no personal income tax, and packages may include housing or transport allowances. Always compare the total package, not just the base salary.
united-arab-emirates.languages: Arabic and English (English is the main business language)
tips: A professional photo on your CV is common and accepted.
Include your nationality and visa status, as employers often ask.
Dress formally and conservatively for interviews.
Build rapport; relationships and respectful manners matter a lot.

japan.name: Japan
japan.summary: Japan is a major advanced economy with global leaders in automotive, electronics and manufacturing. Tokyo, Osaka and Nagoya are the largest job markets.
japan.jobMarket: IT, engineering, manufacturing, healthcare and hospitality face labour shortages due to an ageing population. Software engineers and specialists with Japanese skills are especially valued.
japan.visa: Common routes are the Engineer/Specialist in Humanities/International Services visa, the Highly Skilled Professional points-based visa, and Specified Skilled Worker visas for certain industries. Check the official Immigration Services Agency of Japan website, as requirements change.
japan.salaryNote: Base salaries can be modest compared with the US, but bonuses and allowances are common. Seniority still influences pay at many traditional companies.
japan.languages: Japanese (English-only roles exist mainly in tech and foreign companies)
tips: Traditional companies may expect a standard-format résumé (rirekisho) with a photo.
Politeness, humility and formal greetings are very important.
Arrive early and dress conservatively, typically in a dark suit.
Show long-term commitment and team orientation rather than individual ambition.

singapore.name: Singapore
singapore.summary: Singapore is a leading Asian hub for finance, trade and technology, with a highly international workforce. Many multinationals base their Asia-Pacific headquarters there.
singapore.jobMarket: Finance, technology, logistics, biomedical sciences and professional services are key sectors. Software, data, cybersecurity and finance specialists are in strong demand.
singapore.visa: Professionals usually need an Employment Pass, which considers salary and a points-based framework, while mid-skilled workers may use the S Pass. Criteria are updated regularly, so check the official Ministry of Manpower (MOM) website.
singapore.salaryNote: Salaries in finance and tech are competitive and personal income tax is relatively low. Housing and car ownership are expensive.
singapore.languages: English (the main business language), plus Mandarin, Malay and Tamil
tips: Keep your CV concise and results-focused; a photo is optional.
Be clear about your notice period and work pass status.
Show that you can work across cultures in a diverse team.
Be prepared to discuss expected salary directly, as it's often asked early.

before-reverse-engineer-posting.title: Turn the job ad into a checklist
before-reverse-engineer-posting.body: Highlight every skill and responsibility in the posting and write one example from your experience next to each. Gaps you find now are questions you can prepare for instead of being surprised by.

before-story-bank.title: Build a bank of five stories
before-story-bank.body: Prepare five short stories about a success, a failure, a conflict, a time you led and a time you learned fast. Most behavioral questions can be answered by adapting one of them.

before-news-check.title: Check the latest company news
before-news-check.body: The day before, search for recent news, product launches or funding about the company. Mentioning something current shows real interest and gives you a natural question to ask.

before-map-interviewers.title: Look up your interviewers
before-map-interviewers.body: If you know who will interview you, check their professional profiles to understand their role and background. It helps you tailor examples to what each person cares about.

before-practice-out-loud.title: Practice answers out loud
before-practice-out-loud.body: Rehearsing silently feels fluent, but speaking reveals where you ramble or get stuck. Say your key answers aloud a few times, ideally timing them to one or two minutes.

before-prepare-kit.title: Pack your interview kit
before-prepare-kit.body: Prepare printed copies of your CV, a notebook, a pen, your ID and the interviewer's contact details. Having everything ready the night before removes last-minute stress.

before-plan-route.title: Plan your route with a buffer
before-plan-route.body: Check the travel time at the same hour of day and add at least 20 minutes of buffer. Aim to arrive nearby early and walk in 5 to 10 minutes before the start.

before-thirty-sixty-ninety.title: Sketch a 30-60-90 day plan
before-thirty-sixty-ninety.body: Write a few bullet points on what you would learn, deliver and improve in your first three months. Even if nobody asks, it sharpens your answers about how you would add value.

during-first-ninety-seconds.title: Own the first 90 seconds
during-first-ninety-seconds.body: First impressions form quickly, so greet everyone warmly, smile and use their names. A calm, friendly start makes the rest of the conversation easier for both sides.

during-pause-before-answering.title: Pause before you answer
during-pause-before-answering.body: Taking two or three seconds to think looks confident, not slow. It helps you choose the best example and avoid filling the silence with filler words.

during-numbers-in-answers.title: Put numbers in your answers
during-numbers-in-answers.body: Whenever possible, quantify impact: time saved, revenue grown, errors reduced or customers served. Concrete figures make your stories credible and memorable.

during-clarify-question.title: Clarify unclear questions
during-clarify-question.body: If a question is vague, ask a short clarifying question or restate what you understood. Answering the right question is better than answering quickly.

during-watch-length.title: Keep answers to about two minutes
during-watch-length.body: Long answers lose attention and short ones feel thin. Aim for one to two minutes, then check in with something like: would you like more detail on that?

during-take-notes.title: Take brief notes
during-take-notes.body: Jotting down key points the interviewer mentions shows engagement. You can refer back to them in your questions and in your thank-you message.

during-mirror-energy.title: Match the interviewer's style
during-mirror-energy.body: Notice whether the interviewer is formal or relaxed, fast or thoughtful, and adjust your tone slightly. Matching their pace builds rapport without losing your own personality.

during-close-strong.title: End with a clear close
during-close-strong.body: Before leaving, briefly summarise why you fit the role and confirm your interest. Then ask about the next steps and the expected timeline.

tough-gap-in-cv.title: Explaining a gap in your CV
tough-gap-in-cv.body: Be brief and honest about the reason, whether it was caregiving, health, study or a job search. Then quickly move on to what you did to stay sharp and why you are ready now.

tough-why-leaving.title: Why are you leaving your job?
tough-why-leaving.body: Focus on what you are moving toward, such as growth, new challenges or a better fit, rather than what you are escaping. Never criticise your current or previous employer.

tough-failure-story.title: Tell me about a failure
tough-failure-story.body: Choose a real but recoverable mistake, own your part without excuses, and spend most of the answer on what you learned. Close with how you applied that lesson later.

tough-overqualified.title: You seem overqualified
tough-overqualified.body: Address the hidden concern, which is usually that you will get bored or leave quickly. Explain why this role fits your goals now and how your experience helps the team from day one.

tough-dont-know-answer.title: When you don't know the answer
tough-dont-know-answer.body: Don't bluff. Say what you do know, explain how you would find the rest, and if possible reason through the problem out loud so they can see how you think.

tough-other-offers.title: Are you interviewing elsewhere?
tough-other-offers.body: It's fine to say yes without naming companies or details. Emphasise that this role is a strong match and share any timeline constraints honestly.

tough-illegal-questions.title: Handling inappropriate questions
tough-illegal-questions.body: In many countries, questions about age, religion, marital status or family plans are not allowed. You can politely steer back to your qualifications, for example by saying nothing will affect your ability to do the job.

tough-where-in-five-years.title: Where do you see yourself in five years?
tough-where-in-five-years.body: Show ambition that fits the path this role can offer, such as deeper expertise or more responsibility. Avoid naming a completely different career or the interviewer's own job.

remote-test-tech.title: Test the platform in advance
remote-test-tech.body: Install the video app, update it and do a test call with a friend a day before. Check that your camera, microphone and screen sharing all work on the device you'll use.

remote-camera-eye-level.title: Put the camera at eye level
remote-camera-eye-level.body: Raise your laptop on books or a stand so the camera is level with your eyes. Look at the lens when making key points so it feels like eye contact to the interviewer.

remote-lighting-audio.title: Get lighting and audio right
remote-lighting-audio.body: Face a window or lamp so your face is evenly lit, and avoid bright light behind you. Wired earphones with a microphone usually sound clearer than laptop speakers.

remote-clean-background.title: Choose a calm background
remote-clean-background.body: Sit in front of a tidy, neutral background and remove distractions from the frame. Tell people at home when your interview is and silence notifications on every device.

remote-notes-off-screen.title: Use notes wisely
remote-notes-off-screen.body: A few keywords on a sticky note near the camera can help, but don't read full answers. Interviewers notice when your eyes keep moving across the screen.

remote-lag-etiquette.title: Allow for audio delay
remote-lag-etiquette.body: Wait a beat after the interviewer finishes before you speak to avoid talking over each other. If the connection drops, calmly rejoin and briefly summarise where you were.

remote-backup-plan.title: Have a backup plan
remote-backup-plan.body: Keep your phone charged and the interviewer's contact details handy in case your internet fails. A mobile hotspot ready to go can save the interview.

remote-one-way-video.title: One-way video interviews
remote-one-way-video.body: For recorded interviews without a live person, treat the camera as your audience and smile at the start. Use any practice questions to check framing, then answer with the same energy as a live call.

after-debrief-notes.title: Write a debrief right away
after-debrief-notes.body: Within an hour, note down the questions asked, your answers, names and anything you would improve. These notes help with follow-ups and your next interviews.

after-personal-thank-you.title: Personalise your thank-you note
after-personal-thank-you.body: Send a short thank-you email within 24 hours that mentions one specific topic you discussed. A personal detail makes it memorable instead of generic.

after-follow-up-timing.title: Follow up at the right time
after-follow-up-timing.body: If they gave a timeline, wait until it passes before following up. Otherwise, a polite check-in about a week later is reasonable.

after-connect-linkedin.title: Connect professionally
after-connect-linkedin.body: Consider sending a connection request with a short note to the people you met. Keep it professional and don't use it to ask about the decision.

after-handle-silence.title: Handle silence calmly
after-handle-silence.body: Hiring processes often take longer than planned for reasons that have nothing to do with you. After one or two polite follow-ups, keep your focus on other opportunities.

after-ask-feedback.title: Ask for feedback after a rejection
after-ask-feedback.body: Reply graciously and ask whether they can share one or two things you could improve. Not everyone will answer, but useful feedback is valuable, and a positive reply keeps the door open.

after-compare-offers.title: Compare offers on the full picture
after-compare-offers.body: Look beyond base salary to bonus, benefits, leave, flexibility, growth and commute. Writing them side by side in a table makes the right choice clearer.

after-keep-pipeline.title: Keep your pipeline active
after-keep-pipeline.body: Don't pause your job search while you wait for one company's decision. Continuing to apply keeps your options open and reduces the pressure on any single interview.
